rows.explanation: Paul says both Jews and Gentiles are all under sin, a universal condition much like mankind being in loss.
Scripture has shut all people up under sin, directly describing humanity as subject to a state of loss.
Paul concludes that the whole world is guilty before God, matching the ayah’s sweeping judgment on humanity.
John says the whole world lies in wickedness, describing it as living within a corrupt state.
Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, a universal deficit before God.
The psalm says all have turned aside and none does good, portraying humanity as broadly astray.
The psalm likewise says all have turned aside and none does good.
The image of all people as sheep gone astray gives a collective picture of humanity’s lostness.
The verse says there is no one on earth who always does good without sinning.
The verse sets condemnation for all against the gift of justification and life for all through one righteous act.
Where all die in Adam, the verse says all will be made alive in Christ.
Sin brings death to all people, presenting a universal consequence of humanity’s fallen condition.
The speaker says no living person can be justified in God’s sight, expressing a universal human shortfall.
Solomon’s prayer says there is no one who does not sin.
The merchants shrink measures and falsify balances, depicting a trade in which buyers are made to lose what is due them.
Jesus asks what a person gains by winning the whole world but losing himself.
Jesus contrasts gaining the whole world with losing one’s soul.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world if one loses one’s soul.
The broad road leads to destruction and many enter it, depicting a widespread path toward ruin.
A way that seems right ends in death, matching the reading of loss that can go unnoticed.
The gospel is veiled to those who are lost, describing people as already in a state of ruin.
The believer has eternal life and has passed from death to life, the reverse condition for those who receive it.
Paul says all were shut up in disobedience so that mercy might be shown to all, describing a universal predicament before its remedy.
The speaker says all are unclean, their righteousness is like filthy rags, and their iniquities carry them away.
The account says all flesh had corrupted its way on earth, describing the pervasive corruption of humanity before the flood.
The psalm asks who could stand if God marked iniquities, implying that no one can withstand that judgment.
Sin pays death as its wage, using an account of what a person receives that echoes the ayah’s loss.
Paul says that “we all” were by nature children of wrath, describing a shared former state of condemnation.
Jesus says the unbeliever is condemned already, describing a present state of judgment.
Jesus says he came to seek and save the lost, treating lost people as those needing rescue.
The person who delights in the Lord’s law is like a fruitful tree, and whatever he does prospers, reversing the loss condition for that person.
Paul says God was reconciling the world to himself and not counting its trespasses against it, reversing the state of alienation and guilt.
The readers were once like sheep going astray but have returned to their shepherd, reversing the image of being lost.
